meta.description: Multi-year governance structure and ideological scoring for Australian political parties, with international comparators. Latest scores are at the top level (for scatter plots); history arrays track changes over time (for timeline chart and the dated 'Scoring justification' section, which is rendered entirely from this data — there is no separate hand-written justification text anywhere else). Scores are approximate and deliberately coarse — see project page for full methodology.

left_right.description: Political ideology spectrum. -10 = far left (revolutionary socialist), -5 = social democratic, 0 = centre, +5 = conservative, +10 = far right.

internal_governance.description: Depth and genuineness of member control over party decisions. Composite of leadership selection, candidate preselection, policy platform approval, minority rights, and structural accountability mechanisms. 0 = leader-appointed, closed. 10 = full liquid/sortition/direct member democracy.

external_reform.description: Sustained external advocacy for governance reform — electoral reform, anti-corruption, transparency, accountability mechanisms. 0 = none or opposes reform. 10 = democracy reform is the party's primary platform and purpose.

notability.description: Rough public profile / electoral significance. Not a membership count (those are unreliable). 1 = marginal, virtually unknown. 5 = established minor party. 10 = government-forming major party.

meta.history_entry_schema: Each history entry carries the three scores at that date plus, for each dimension (left_right, internal_governance, external_reform), a '<dimension>_note' explaining the score and a '<dimension>_sources' array of {label, url} citations. sources may be an empty array when a note describes context/continuity rather than a citable claim.

parties.name: Australian Labor Party
parties.note: Faction-controlled preselections despite formal OMOV rules; weighted parliamentarian votes in some selections; internal reform pushes (Leigh, Faulkner) stalled.

history.left_right_note: Centre-left, social democratic — Whitlam-era positioning slightly further left than the modern party.
history.internal_note: Whitlam becomes leader, pushing reform of party structure away from pure union control toward broader branch membership input — though federal conference remains union-dominated (the '36 faceless men' image).
history.external_note: No governance-reform advocacy at this stage.

history.left_right_note: Centre-left, social democratic under Hawke — settles at the party's modern position.
history.internal_note: Hawke government. Factional system formalised at national level (Left, Centre-Left, Right). Candidate selection increasingly determined by factional deals rather than open member contests.
history.external_note: No governance-reform advocacy at this stage.

history.left_right_note: No ideological shift from the Hawke/Keating era.
history.internal_note: Rudd elected PM on a platform of internal party reform and greater member engagement; some state branches experiment with OMOV preselections, but factional control persists federally.
history.external_note: No governance-reform advocacy at this stage.

history.internal_note: Rudd rolled by Gillard in a factional leadership coup; factions reassert control and the internal reform agenda is sidelined.
history.external_note: No governance-reform advocacy at this stage.

history.internal_note: Rudd returns and pushes major internal reforms including stronger OMOV provisions for leadership and preselection; John Faulkner's reform agenda gains brief traction.
history.external_note: No governance-reform advocacy at this stage.

history.internal_note: Post-election loss; reforms largely stall and the factional duopoly re-establishes itself. Andrew Leigh later publicly criticises the 'duopoly' (2023).

internal_sources.label: Andrew Leigh calls out Labor's factional duopoly (The Conversation, 2023)

history.external_note: No governance-reform advocacy at this stage.

history.internal_note: Factional preselection control persists; no structural internal reform accompanies this period.
history.external_note: National Anti-Corruption Commission Act enacted — but the 'exceptional circumstances' public-hearings threshold is criticised by Transparency International Australia and the Centre for Public Integrity as too restrictive.

external_sources.label: Joint statement on the NACC Bill 2022

history.internal_note: Faction-controlled preselections persist despite formal OMOV rules; weighted parliamentarian votes remain in some selections; internal reform pushes from Andrew Leigh and John Faulkner have stalled.

internal_sources.label: Andrew Leigh calls out Labor's factional duopoly (The Conversation, 2023)

history.external_note: NACC has held 25+ private hearings and zero public hearings as of Dec 2025. Donation disclosure reforms were legislated in 2025.

parties.name: Liberal Party / Coalition
parties.note: Opposed real-time donation disclosure (2019); opposed truth-in-advertising bill; 2018/19 integrity commission proposal widely criticised as designed to hold only private hearings.

history.left_right_note: Centre-right, conservative — founding-era positioning slightly further right than the modern party.
history.internal_note: Founded by Menzies. Branch-based structure but elite-dominated; preselection controlled by state executives, not broad membership.
history.external_note: No governance-reform advocacy at this stage.

history.left_right_note: Centre-right, conservative under Fraser — settles at the party's modern position.
history.internal_note: Fraser era. Centralised party control; branch stacking becomes entrenched practice in NSW and Queensland.
history.external_note: No governance-reform advocacy at this stage.

history.internal_note: Howard era ends. Preselection remains faction/executive-controlled. No significant internal governance reform.
history.external_note: No governance-reform advocacy at this stage.

history.internal_note: No internal governance change recorded at this point.
history.external_note: Federal director calls real-time donation disclosure 'too onerous'. Party opposes the truth-in-advertising bill.

history.internal_note: Leader/elite-controlled preselections persist; branch stacking remains entrenched in some states.
history.external_note: No positive governance-reform record found. The 2018/19 integrity commission proposal was widely criticised as designed to hold only private hearings, with no public tip-off pathway.

parties.name: Australian Greens
parties.note: Leadership not member-elected in all jurisdictions; varied preselection processes by state. Strong external record: 10-year federal anti-corruption campaign, truth-in-advertising bill, donation cap advocacy.

history.internal_note: Founded from a merger of state-based green parties. Decentralised federation model — state branches retain significant autonomy; leadership and preselection processes vary by state.
history.external_note: Early platform includes proportional representation and donation reform.

history.internal_note: No internal structural change recorded at this point.
history.external_note: First federal lower house seat (Adam Bandt, Melbourne). A federal anti-corruption body campaign begins to take shape; donation-reform advocacy intensifies.

history.internal_note: Internal governance unchanged — leadership still not universally member-elected.
history.external_note: NACC bill passes the Senate with Greens amendments (inspector oversight powers) — a 10-year campaign delivers a concrete win.

external_sources.label: NACC bill passes Senate — Greens release

history.internal_note: Leadership is still not member-elected in all jurisdictions; preselection processes vary by state; member input on policy platform is stronger than on candidate/leadership selection.
history.external_note: Strongest external reform record of any Australian parliamentary party: the NACC win above, a truth-in-political-advertising bill modelled on South Australia's law, and a sustained "Clean Up Politics" donations-cap/contractor-donor-ban campaign.

external_sources.label: Truth in political advertising — Greens ACT

parties.name: Victorian Socialists
parties.note: Constitutional OMOV (adopted Jan 2024); competitive conference elections with minority faction platform rights; electorate-based branch structure. No external reform advocacy — revolutionary, not reformist (does not believe parliament can be meaningfully reformed under capitalism).

history.left_right_note: Far left, revolutionary socialist; abolition of capitalism as stated goal.
history.internal_note: Estimate — prior to formal constitutional OMOV. Party had a de facto democratic culture and volunteer-based structure, but formal member-governance mechanisms were not yet codified in the constitution. Verify with party records.
history.external_note: No external governance-reform advocacy.

history.internal_note: Constitutional OMOV and party democracy adopted at the Jan 2024 conference. Aims document adopted as part of the new constitution: "commitment to party democracy, freedom of debate and the principle of one member one vote."
history.external_note: No external governance-reform advocacy — deliberate: VS holds that parliament cannot be meaningfully reformed under capitalism.

history.internal_note: Electorate-based branch structures adopted at the June 2025 conference (360 attendees). Competitive faction platform demonstrated: the Communist Caucus ran an alternative leadership slate, was given platform time, and lost at the vote.

internal_sources.label: Victorian Socialists conference resolves to expand party organisation — Red Flag

history.external_note: No external governance-reform advocacy.

history.left_right_note: Far left, revolutionary socialist; abolition of capitalism as stated goal.
history.internal_note: Reassessed from an earlier heartbeat finding of "too thin" after counter-feedback from a VS member pointing to the constitutional OMOV mechanism and its June 2025 competitive-faction test above.
history.external_note: No external governance-reform advocacy. This is deliberate: VS holds that parliament cannot be meaningfully reformed under capitalism, so external advocacy takes the form of building a democratic workers' movement rather than patching existing institutions. The party's aims document describes a democratic-socialist vision (recall rights, no special privileges for elected reps, political pluralism) but does not advocate reform of existing parliamentary institutions.

parties.name: One Nation
parties.note: Leader-dominated structure. AEC compliance action forced withdrawal of $800k+ contested election-spending claims (June 2026).

history.internal_note: Founded by Pauline Hanson after her expulsion from the Liberal Party. Leader-dominated from inception; no member primaries or competitive internal ballots.
history.external_note: No governance-reform advocacy at this stage.

history.internal_note: AEC deregistration after a court found the party's registration relied on misrepresented membership numbers; public leadership feud between Hanson, David Oldfield and David Ettridge over control of the party. Reinforces clique/leader control rather than member governance.
history.external_note: No governance-reform advocacy at this stage.

history.internal_note: Federal resurgence: four senators elected at the 2016 double-dissolution election. Leader-dominated structure persists — several elected senators (e.g. Rodney Culleton, Brian Burston) subsequently split from the party citing centralised control.
history.external_note: No governance-reform advocacy at this stage.

history.internal_note: Leader-dominated; the party constitution gives Hanson near-total control.
history.external_note: AEC compliance action forced withdrawal of $800k+ in contested election-spending claims after roughly 140 unjustified items, June 2026 — cuts against, rather than advances, governance reform.

parties.name: Jacqui Lambie Network
parties.note: Sustained integrity-body criticism since 2018; donations-disclosure bill on party site.

history.internal_note: Founded by Jacqui Lambie after departing the Palmer United Party. Personality-centred structure from the outset.
history.external_note: Broad populist platform, not yet focused specifically on integrity/accountability mechanisms.

history.internal_note: Centralised around Lambie; limited evidence of structured member democracy.
history.external_note: Lambie re-elected to the Senate under the JLN banner, having been removed from parliament in 2017 by the Section 44 dual-citizenship crisis. Integrity-body criticism (begun 2018) is now an established, sustained position.

history.internal_note: Centralised around Lambie; limited evidence of structured member democracy.
history.external_note: Sustained criticism of integrity-body design since 2018, including the Coalition's CIC proposal ('lap dog with dentures'). A donations-disclosure bill is on the party site; its parliamentary progress is not independently verified.

external_sources.label: Canberra Times — Lambie lashes proposed corruption watchdog

parties.name: Katter's Australian Party
parties.note: Decentralisation calls and NQ partition referendum — policy positions, not sustained reform program.

history.internal_note: Founded by long-serving independent MP Bob Katter. Family/leader-centred control from the outset.
history.external_note: Decentralisation of federal departments is already part of the founding platform.

history.internal_note: Electoral high-water mark: wins seats at the Queensland state election, including Bob Katter's son Robbie Katter — reinforcing family-centred control of the party.
history.external_note: No change to the party's external reform posture at this point.

history.internal_note: Leader-dominated; the Katter family remains central to party identity and control.
history.external_note: Decentralisation calls and the North Queensland partition referendum are policy positions, not a sustained governance-reform program.

parties.name: Pirate Party Australia
parties.note: Liquid democracy culture; merged into Fusion Party's federated structure 2021. Democracy and transparency reform is the party's reason for existing.

history.left_right_note: Centre-left, digital rights and transparency platform, from founding.
history.internal_note: Founded as part of the international Pirate Party movement. Liquid democracy culture was part of the platform from inception.
history.external_note: Digital-rights and transparency reform were part of the platform from inception.

history.internal_note: First federal election contest with Senate candidates across multiple states, built on the liquid-democracy platform.
history.external_note: Campaign builds profile around transparency reform.

history.internal_note: Voluntarily deregisters as an independent AEC party and merges into the Fusion Party's federated structure, continuing as a distinct internal grouping with its own membership and infrastructure.

internal_sources.label: DOD org page — PPAU status note

history.external_note: No change to reform focus through the merger.

history.left_right_note: Centre-left, digital rights and transparency platform.
history.internal_note: Liquid-democracy culture and participatory governance traditions continue from the international Pirate Party movement. Merged into Fusion Party's federated structure in 2021; continues as a distinct internal grouping.

internal_sources.label: DOD org page — PPAU status note

history.external_note: Democracy and transparency reform is the party's reason for existing. Initiated the Electoral Royal Commission campaign.

parties.name: Fusion Party
parties.note: Federation of minor parties (incl. Pirate Party Australia) formed in response to 2021 legislation raising the minimum party-membership threshold from 500 to 1,500. Federated structure — member parties retain autonomy as formal branches. Platform includes an anti-corruption commission, political-donations disclosure above $1,000, and whistleblower protections.
parties.scoring_note: Fusion's own website (fusionparty.org.au) returned 403 Forbidden to automated fetches during scoring — internal_governance is sourced from Wikipedia's description of the federated structure only, not the party's own governance documents. Treat that score as more provisional than most other entries on this page.

history.left_right_note: Left, progressive/secular-humanist — inherited from founding member parties (Pirate, Secular, Science, Climate Emergency).
history.internal_note: Formation triggered by the Electoral Legislation Amendment (Party Registration Integrity) Bill 2021, which raised the minimum non-parliamentary party membership threshold from 500 to 1,500 — forcing several small parties to amalgamate rather than independently meet the new bar. Pirate Party Australia deregisters as an independent AEC party this month and joins the federated structure as a founding member, retaining its own membership and infrastructure.
history.external_note: No electoral test yet at this point — governance-reform platform (see 2022-03 entry) still forming as constituent parties merge.

history.internal_note: Science Party and Secular Party deregister (Jan 2022) and merge in; the amalgamation renames to "FUSION: Science, Pirate, Secular, Climate Emergency," formalising the federated structure with each origin party retaining a degree of autonomy as a formal branch.
history.external_note: Platform crystallises around transparent government (donations disclosure above $1,000, open access to policy advice), an anti-corruption commission, whistleblower protections, network neutrality, and a constitutional bill of rights — a genuinely multi-front governance-reform platform, though not yet tested at the ballot box.

history.internal_note: No structural change recorded at this point.
history.external_note: First electoral test: Senate candidates in every mainland state at the 2022 federal election, 51,676 votes nationally (0.34%); best lower-house result 2.16% in the Division of Dobell. No candidates elected.

history.internal_note: Federated structure persists — member parties (including Pirate Party Australia) retain autonomy as formal branches. Renamed "FUSION | Planet Rescue | Whistleblower Protection | Innovation" in Jan 2025; formed a 2025 alliance with the Australian Progressives and Democracy First.
history.external_note: Governance-reform platform unchanged (anti-corruption commission, donations disclosure, whistleblower protections, lower voting age to 16). Ran candidates in six states/territories at the 2025 federal election; none elected — still no legislative track record to point to, unlike Greens' NACC amendments.

parties.name: Australian Democrats
parties.note: Re-established. Advocates citizens' assembly for Vic upper house reform; proportional representation; evidence-based approach citing 2025 AES data.

history.left_right_note: Centre, founded as a liberal/moderate alternative to the two major blocs.
history.internal_note: Founded by Don Chipp on an explicit government-accountability platform ("keep the bastards honest"). First Australian party to let the whole membership elect the leader by postal ballot and to put policy to binding member ballots — genuine OMOV, novel for its time.
history.external_note: Founding purpose was explicitly a government-accountability watchdog role, using the party's Senate balance-of-power position to scrutinise legislation.

history.internal_note: Leader Meg Lees negotiates a GST deal with the Howard government despite a prior member ballot opposing it — a real test of the party's binding-plebiscite mechanism. The backlash split the party: Lees was deposed as leader by Natasha Stott Despoja in 2001, then quit the party entirely in 2002 to sit as an independent — the mechanism could actually bind and remove a leader, for better or worse.
history.external_note: No change to external reform posture recorded at this point.

history.internal_note: A decade of leadership spills and resignations following the 1999 GST split culminates in the 2007 federal election, where the party's remaining four Senators lose their seats (terms expiring 30 June 2008) — leaving the Democrats with no federal representation for the first time since 1977. The binding-ballot mechanism nominally persists but has no functioning parliamentary party left to discipline.
history.external_note: Losing all Senate seats ends the party's balance-of-power watchdog role — the mechanism through which its 1977 accountability platform was actually exercised.

history.left_right_note: No ideological shift — party is dormant/defunct at this point.
history.internal_note: Deregistered by the AEC (28 November 2016) after failing to maintain the minimum-membership threshold — the original party ceases to legally exist.

internal_sources.label: AEC deregistration notice, Nov 2016 (via Wikipedia citation)

history.external_note: No governance-reform activity — the party is legally deregistered.

history.left_right_note: Centre — re-registers as a fresh general-purpose small party.
history.internal_note: Re-registered with the AEC (7 April 2019) after merging with CountryMinded. This is the re-established party referred to throughout this page — it does not carry forward the original's binding whole-membership ballot mechanisms; internal governance resets to standard party structures.

internal_sources.label: AEC registration decision, Apr 2019 (via Wikipedia citation)

history.external_note: Freshly re-registered and not yet focused on a specific governance-reform campaign.

history.internal_note: Standard party structures; limited evidence of member governance beyond electoral processes. Notably lower than the original party (1977–2016, see above), which pioneered whole-membership postal-ballot leader elections and binding policy plebiscites — the re-established party does not carry those mechanisms forward.
history.external_note: Advocates a randomly selected citizens' assembly for Victoria's upper house electoral reform and proportional representation, with evidence-based framing citing 2025 Australian Election Study data (48% support for citizens' assemblies).

external_sources.label: Victoria's Upper House inquiry: the case for a citizens' assembly (DOD blog, May 2026)

parties.name: Flux Party
parties.note: Issue-Based Direct Democracy (two-token economy, abstention-as-capital, proportional delegation). Deregistered. Included for historical comparison of governance innovation.
parties.scoring_note: Scored August 2026 based on platform during the party's active period, 2016–2022.

history.internal_note: Registered with the AEC. Issue-Based Direct Democracy as founding platform: two-token economy (votes + political capital), abstention rewarded as political capital, proportional delegation with revocation. Most sophisticated internal governance design of any Australian party.

internal_sources.label: Issue-Based Direct Democracy — DOD concept page

history.external_note: Democracy reform was the entire platform from founding.

history.left_right_note: No ideological shift through to deregistration.
history.internal_note: Deregistered by the AEC. The IBDD mechanism was unchanged throughout the party's active period. Included here for historical comparison of governance innovation.
history.external_note: Democracy reform remained the entire platform through deregistration.

parties.name: MiVote

logo.source: https://www.designingopendemocracy.com/organisations/mivote/ (extracted from MiVote's own "Values & Vision" PDF, sourced via Wayback Machine)

parties.note: Four-destination policy model; research-to-voter information pipeline with university research, domain experts, advisory committees, and ethics committee sign-off; 60% supermajority threshold; mandatory mandate binding Senate candidates to member vote. Deregistered ~2019.
parties.scoring_note: Scored August 2026 based on platform during the party's active period, 2014–2019.

history.left_right_note: Centre, non-partisan framing, from founding. Political sibling of Flux Party — both launched 2014–2016 with complementary democracy-reform designs.
history.internal_note: Founded by Adam Jacoby. Structured information pipeline, four-destination policy model (not yes/no), 60% supermajority threshold, mandatory mandate. Constitutional requirement that elected senators vote according to the aggregated member position.
history.external_note: Democracy reform was the entire platform from founding.

history.left_right_note: No ideological shift through to deregistration.
history.internal_note: Deregistered ~2019 without electing senators. MiVote Technologies continued in the UK. Included here for historical comparison alongside Flux Party — political siblings with complementary governance designs.

internal_sources.label: Catching up with Adam Jacoby (DOD podcast, 2021)

history.external_note: Democracy reform remained the entire platform through deregistration.

parties.name: Democratic Labor Party (1955–1978)
parties.note: Formed by the 1955 Labor Split. Directed Senate preferences to keep the ALP from federal power for 17 years. Effective control sat with B. A. Santamaria's National Civic Council rather than the ordinary membership. Wound up 1978; a separate DLP was later re-founded by former members and remains a minor party today — not the entity scored here.

history.left_right_note: Centre-right, anti-communist Catholic-labour breakaway — economically closer to Labor's welfare-state instincts than to the Liberals, but firmly conservative on Cold War foreign policy and social issues.
history.internal_note: Formed as the Australian Labor Party (Anti-Communist) after Victorian federal and state MPs aligned with B. A. Santamaria's anti-communist 'Movement' (later the National Civic Council) were expelled from the ALP at its 1955 Hobart conference. Strategy and direction ran through Santamaria's externally based Movement/NCC rather than ordinary party ballots — an unusual structure: neither leader-dominated nor member-controlled in the usual sense, but directed by a non-elected outside body.
history.external_note: No governance-reform advocacy — founding purpose was anti-communism and Cold War foreign policy, not electoral or accountability mechanisms.

history.internal_note: No change to the party's externally directed structure.
history.external_note: DLP preferences hand Liberal candidate Billy Snedden a paper-thin win in Bruce, denying Labor the two seats it needed to topple the Coalition at the 1961 election — the clearest demonstration of the party's preference-direction strategy actually determining a federal government, though this is electoral tactics rather than governance-mechanism reform.

history.internal_note: Prime Minister Whitlam appoints DLP Senate leader Vince Gair as ambassador to Ireland, a deliberate move to split the party and remove its most effective figure; the DLP loses all its Senate seats at the 1974 election.
history.external_note: With no remaining parliamentary representation, the preference-direction strategy that was the party's only real lever loses its force.

history.left_right_note: No ideological shift through to wind-up.
history.internal_note: Queensland and South Australian branches dissolve in 1976; the party contests only Victoria without success at the 1977 election and formally winds up in 1978. (A separate Democratic Labor Party was later founded by former members and continues today — not the entity scored here.)
history.external_note: Defunct.

parties.name: United Australia Party (1931–1945)
parties.note: Governing conservative party of the 1930s–40s; direct predecessor of the modern Liberal Party. No relation to the unrelated modern minor party of the same name (est. 2013).

history.left_right_note: Centre-right, formed by fiscally conservative Labor defectors merging with the Nationalist Party in response to the Great Depression.
history.internal_note: Six Labor MPs who opposed the Scullin government's Depression-era financial policy, led by former Tasmanian Premier Joseph Lyons, merged with the Nationalist Party. Lyons was chosen as leader for his public popularity rather than through a member ballot — a top-down formation from the outset.
history.external_note: No governance-reform advocacy — founding platform was fiscal orthodoxy in response to the Depression.

history.internal_note: Landslide victory at the 1931 federal election gives the UAP an outright House of Representatives majority in its first contest — Lyons becomes PM.
history.external_note: No governance-reform advocacy.

history.internal_note: Lyons dies in office; the parliamentary party elects Robert Menzies as leader and PM. Leadership continues to be decided by the parliamentary party, not the wider membership.
history.external_note: No governance-reform advocacy.

history.left_right_note: No ideological shift through to dissolution.
history.internal_note: The UAP ceases to exist as a parliamentary party; its members join the newly formed Liberal Party of Australia, which absorbs its position and much of its base.
history.external_note: Defunct.

parties.name: Australia Party (1969–1986)
parties.note: Grew out of a Liberal Party splinter opposed to Vietnam War conscription. Most members and infrastructure merged into the newly formed Australian Democrats in 1977 — its clearest governance-reform legacy is the party it fed into, more than its own program.

history.left_right_note: Centre-left/centrist, formed from a Liberal Party splinter opposed to conscription and the Vietnam War.
history.internal_note: Independent Senator Reg Turnbull merges his supporters with Gordon Barton's Australian Reform Movement to form the Australia Party, contested 'convenor' leadership positions from early on.
history.external_note: Platform to liberalise abortion law, end conscription, eliminate censorship, and protect the environment — civil-liberties and policy reform rather than governance-mechanism reform specifically.

history.internal_note: Turnbull resigns after former Australian Reform Movement members accuse Gordon Barton's leadership of acting undemocratically by conducting secret negotiations — an early, documented internal-governance flashpoint.
history.external_note: No change to reform platform.

history.internal_note: Best electoral result to date; contested 'national convenor' leadership elections continue (Siddons defeats Gilfillan for the role in 1974).
history.external_note: Directs preferences to Labor, helping end 23 years of Coalition government at the 1972 election — a real governance effect achieved through preference tactics rather than a reform platform.

history.internal_note: Most members and organisational infrastructure merge into the newly formed Australian Democrats; former Australia Party convenors John Siddons and Colin Mason are later elected as Democrats senators. A residual Australia Party structure continued in a reduced form until 1986.
history.external_note: Its civil-liberties and reform-minded membership base becomes part of the Democrats' founding coalition alongside the New Liberal Movement.

parties.name: Your Party
parties.note: Sortition-selected founding conference delegates (via Sortition Foundation) — one of few parties globally using random selection for internal deliberative bodies. International comparator. General-purpose progressive platform alongside democratic reform.

history.internal_note: Founding conference delegates selected by sortition via the Sortition Foundation: a stratified random sample balanced across gender, region, age, ethnicity, disability, and LGBTQ+ status. One of few parties globally using random selection for internal deliberative bodies. Future conferences are to include a portion of sortition-selected delegates alongside branch-elected delegates.
history.external_note: Democratic reform is in the platform (electoral reform, transparency), but the party is also a general-purpose multi-issue party rather than a single-issue reform party.

external_sources.label: Your Party is using sortition (DOD blog, Dec 2025)
